title: On atheism
subtitle: The fool hath said in his heart, There is no God.
summary: The classical and contemporary denial of God, and the Orthodox answer: that the order, intelligibility, and contingency of the world, and the moral and personal depths of man, point beyond themselves to their uncreated Cause, whom the Church knows not as a conclusion of argument only but as the living God.

essay.text: Atheism is the claim that there is no God: that the universe and all within it, including the mind that asks the question, came to be and will pass away with no uncreated source, no purpose given from beyond, and no judge. In its older form it was rare and argued; in its modern form it is often assumed as the default of an educated age, and dressed in the prestige of the natural sciences. The Church answers it not with contempt for the questioner, for many come to unbelief through real suffering or real disappointment with those who bore the Name, but with the witness of reason and of the saints.
What the world itself says

The first answer is the one the Scriptures themselves give: the creation declares its Maker. That the world exists at all rather than nothing, that it is ordered and not chaos, that its order is intelligible to the mind so that it can be studied, and that none of the things in it carries the cause of its own being within itself, all of this points beyond the world to a cause that is not itself caused, not contingent, not one more thing among things. The Fathers did not argue God into existence as a missing gear in the machine; they read the machine as a word, and asked who spoke it.

The sciences describe how things behave; they do not, and cannot, account for why there is anything to behave at all, nor why its laws should be lawful, nor why a mind should arise within it able to know them. To answer the question of existence with the description of mechanism is to mistake the grammar of the question. The believer and the unbeliever may look at the same data; they differ on what the data is a sign of.
The floor an argument stands on

There is a further line of thought worth setting out slowly, because it does not look at the world so much as at the act of arguing about it. Every argument, on any subject, presupposes certain things before it begins. It presupposes that words hold their meaning from one sentence to the next. It presupposes that a claim and its denial cannot both be true, in the same sense, at the same time. It presupposes that the person listening is bound by the same rules as the person speaking. These are the laws of thought: that a thing is what it is, that it cannot both be and not be, that a statement is either true or false. Nobody arrives at them by investigation. Everyone who investigates anything is already using them.

Notice what sort of thing they are. They have no weight, no location, no colour; no instrument detects them; they were not different in an earlier geological era and are not different in another galaxy. They do not behave like matter, which changes, and they do not behave like the customs of a people, which vary. They are invariant, and they hold whether or not anyone happens to be thinking about them. Whatever else may be said, an account of reality made only of changing physical stuff has not yet said what these are, or why they should hold.

The Christian reading of this is not an embarrassed patch. It is what the Church has meant by the Logos from the beginning. The world is intelligible because it was spoken. Reason in us can find reason in things because neither is the source of the other, and both derive from Reason that is uncreated. St Athanasius put it in a sentence: if the universe were borne along without plan a man might fairly disbelieve, but if it holds together in reason and wisdom and skill, then the One who ordered it is none other than the Word of God. On this reading the laws of thought are not free-standing objects lying about alongside God; they are the way an eternal Mind is, and our thinking is a small participation in it.

There is a smaller point here that is often made loudly and is better made quietly. Anyone who argues that the laws of thought do not hold must use them in order to argue it, and so cannot get the denial started. That is a real observation, but it should not be mistaken for a proof of God. All it shows is that these laws are presupposed and not concluded, that they are the floor and not one of the objects standing on it. What the floor rests on is a further question, and it is exactly the question an enquirer is entitled to press.
The strongest reply, and an honest answer

A thoughtful person who does not believe in God has answers here, and they deserve to be stated at full strength rather than in a weak form that is easy to knock over. The first is that logic is a convention: a set of rules adopted because reasoning with them works, no more mysterious than a system of notation. The second is that the laws of thought are abstract, neither physical nor mental, obtaining necessarily the way mathematical truths obtain, and needing no mind to hold them any more than the number seven needs one. The third and deepest is that they are simply a brute feature of any reality whatsoever, and that the believer has not escaped bruteness at all but only stopped one step later, at God, and called the stopping place an explanation. If it is permissible to stop at an eternal Mind that requires no further account, why is it not permissible to stop at an intelligible world that requires no further account?

Each of these costs something, and it is fairer to name the cost than to declare a victory. If logic is only a convention, then calling an argument true means calling it well played, and the unbeliever has spent the very currency he was using to buy the conclusion that there is no God; that is a hard position to hold consistently, and few who state it really mean it. If the laws of thought are abstract necessities standing on their own, the trouble is not that this is absurd but that it is expensive: a purely physical brain must somehow be in contact with realities that do nothing and cause nothing, and there must be some reason why our reasoning should track them rather than merely be useful. The third reply is the serious one, and it deserves a serious answer rather than a slogan. The Christian answer is that the two stopping places are not of the same kind. To stop at a bare fact is to stop at something that might as easily have been otherwise and has nothing in it that answers to reason. To stop at a Mind is to stop at the one kind of thing in which truths can be held, intended, and known. That is a judgment about which terminus is the more intelligible. It is not a demonstration, and it should be offered as what it is.

A related argument is sometimes pressed harder than it will bear. It is said that if our minds are only the product of selection for survival, we have no reason to trust their conclusions, including the conclusion that there is no God. The reply is that creatures who see the world roughly as it is tend to survive better than creatures who do not, so selection does favour a good deal of accuracy. That reply is largely right and should be granted. What survives it is narrower and more interesting: selection favours what works, and what works and what is true run together closely where survival is at stake and much less closely in abstract matters far from it, which is precisely where the arguments about God are conducted. That is a reason for humility on every side of the question. It is not a reason for anyone to stop reasoning.
Meaning in a world of matter

A second thread runs alongside the first. Physical things have physical properties: mass, charge, position. Thoughts have a property hard to state in that vocabulary, namely that they are about something. A thought of justice, or of a friend who died, or of the year 1204, reaches beyond itself to what it is of. Whether that aboutness can be built out of physical relations is one of the genuinely open questions in the philosophy of mind, and it would be dishonest to call it settled; there are careful accounts on which representation is a matter of causal and functional relations and nothing more. The Christian suggestion is not that such accounts are foolish but that they may be derivative all the way down. A map means a country because someone means it so. St Gregory of Nyssa, describing the ingenious water organs of his day, made the point that nobody supposes the bronze shaped itself or the air sounded the pipe of its own motion, and that the mind behind such a device is proved by the device while never being visible in it. If everything that means anything means it by derivation, then something must mean underivedly, and that is what the Church calls the Logos.
The witness within man

There is a second witness, nearer than the stars: the moral and personal depth of man himself. The sense that some things are owed and others forbidden, not by mere preference but in truth; the hunger for a meaning that death does not cancel; the experience of conscience as a voice and not only a feeling; the capacity for love that gives itself away, all of these strain against a world that is only matter in motion. They are, the Fathers taught, the image of God in man, answering to its Origin.

This too is often put as an argument, and it too needs handling with care. If right and wrong are only what a species came to prefer, then cruelty is not evil but merely unhelpful, and almost nobody can hold that line when they meet real cruelty. The observation is worth making. What it does not license is any suggestion that unbelievers are not good, which is false, insulting, and contradicted by ordinary experience; many atheists live better than many Christians. The question is never who behaves well. It is what makes the behaviour good, and whether the indignation everyone feels at torture is tracking something real or only reporting a preference. And there is an old objection here that deserves a plain answer: is a thing good because God commands it, or does God command it because it is good? Neither, as the Orthodox tradition frames it. God's commands are not arbitrary decrees, nor is He measuring Himself against a standard set above Him. They express what He is, and He is the Good itself, so that goodness is not a rule He obeys or a rule He invents, but His own nature made known.

None of this compels, and it is not meant to. An argument that cornered a person would not produce faith; it would produce a cornered person. What these considerations do is clear away the impression that unbelief is the neutral, cost-free default and belief the only position with something to explain. Both are positions. Both are paying for something. Both deserve to be examined with the same seriousness and the same patience. St Justin Martyr, writing to pagans in a century when Christians were being executed, still insisted that whatever was rightly said among all men belongs to Christians. That is the posture to argue from.

The Orthodox answer, finally, is not a proof but a Person. The Church does not chiefly reason men into the existence of a first cause; she introduces them to the living God, known in prayer, in the Mysteries, in the lives of the saints who shine with a light not their own. The arguments clear the ground and answer the objector; the knowledge of God is given in the encounter. Come and see, the Gospel says, and many who could not be argued out of their unbelief have been loved out of it.

florilegium.author: St Athanasius the Great
florilegium.text: For if the movement of creation were irrational, and the universe were borne along without plan, a man might fairly disbelieve what we say. But if it subsist in reason and wisdom and skill, and is perfectly ordered throughout, it follows that He that is over it and has ordered it is none other than the [reason or] Word of God.
florilegium.gloss: The hinge of the whole case, and it is fourth century, not modern. Athanasius does not argue that the world is too complicated to have happened on its own. He argues that it is rational, and that rationality is the signature of Reason. The bracketed words are the NPNF translator's, rendering the double sense of Logos.

florilegium.author: St Athanasius the Great
florilegium.text: For just as though some musician, having tuned a lyre, and by his art adjusted the high notes to the low, and the intermediate notes to the rest, were to produce a single tune as the result, so also the Wisdom of God, handling the Universe as a lyre, and adjusting things in the air to things on the earth, and things in the heaven to things in the air, and combining parts into wholes and moving them all by His beck and will, produces well and fittingly, as the result, the unity of the universe and of its order.
florilegium.gloss: The image is worth sitting with. A tuned lyre is not a heap of strings that happens to sound well together. The harmony is the presence of the musician in the instrument, and Athanasius means the comparison strictly: order in the world is not a lucky property of the world but the Word at work in it.

florilegium.author: St Basil the Great
florilegium.text: It is right that any one beginning to narrate the formation of the world should begin with the good order which reigns in visible things. I am about to speak of the creation of heaven and earth, which was not spontaneous, as some have imagined, but drew its origin from God.
florilegium.gloss: Basil opens the whole account of creation not with matter but with order, and names in the same breath the alternative he is refusing. The word he refuses is spontaneous, which is the ancient name for what the modern objector calls chance.

florilegium.author: St Basil the Great
florilegium.text: Those who were too ignorant to rise to a knowledge of a God, could not allow that an intelligent cause presided at the birth of the Universe; a primary error that involved them in sad consequences.
florilegium.gloss: Written against the atomists of Basil's own day, not against ours, and the difference matters. His charge is not that they studied nature too closely. It is that they would not allow an intelligent cause at the beginning of it, and then had to build everything else on that refusal.

florilegium.author: St John of Damascus
florilegium.work: An Exposition of the Orthodox Faith
florilegium.text: For we shall not attribute such a power to the spontaneous. For, supposing their coming into existence was due to the spontaneous; what of the power that put all in order? And let us grant this, if you please. What of that which has preserved and kept them in harmony with the original laws of their existence? Clearly it is something quite distinct from the spontaneous.
florilegium.gloss: The Damascene grants his opponent the move and then asks what it bought. Suppose things did arise of themselves. That still leaves the ordering unexplained, and then the keeping in order unexplained after that. It is the cleanest patristic statement of why accidentalism has to keep paying.

florilegium.author: St John of Damascus
florilegium.work: An Exposition of the Orthodox Faith
florilegium.text: And even the very continuity of the creation, and its preservation and government, teach us that there does exist a Deity, who supports and maintains and preserves and ever provides for this universe.
florilegium.gloss: Not only that the world began, but that it is still here and still coherent. For the Fathers, preservation is an argument in its own right, and not merely an appendix to origination.

florilegium.author: St John of Damascus
florilegium.work: An Exposition of the Orthodox Faith
florilegium.text: So then this one and only God is not Wordless. And possessing the Word, He will have it not as without a subsistence, nor as having had a beginning, nor as destined to cease to be. For there never was a time when God was not Word: but He ever possesses His own Word, begotten of Himself.
florilegium.gloss: Where the Logos enters. God is not Wordless, and the Word is not a faculty God happens to have but a Person God eternally begets. This is the ground a Christian is standing on when he says that reason is not an accident.

florilegium.author: St Gregory of Nyssa
florilegium.work: On the Soul and the Resurrection
florilegium.text: Is it not clearly proved by such visible results that there is a mind of some kind in man, something other than that which is visible, which, by virtue of an invisible thinking nature of its own, first prepares by inward invention such devices, and then, when they have been so matured, brings them to the light and exhibits them in the subservient matter?
florilegium.gloss: St Macrina is answering a materialist objection with the water organs of the fourth century, the nearest thing her age had to a machine that seems to think. Her point is the one the modern comparison with computers keeps running into: the device does not explain itself, and points back to a mind nowhere visible in the bronze.

florilegium.author: St Gregory of Nyssa
florilegium.work: On the Soul and the Resurrection
florilegium.text: The Creation proclaims outright the Creator; for the very heavens, as the Prophet says, declare the glory of God with their unutterable words.
florilegium.gloss: Spoken in a dialogue about grief and death, not in a debating hall. The Fathers did not keep this argument in a separate room from the rest of life, and it is worth noticing where they reached for it.

florilegium.author: St Theophilus of Antioch
florilegium.text: For as the soul in man is not seen, being invisible to men, but is perceived through the motion of the body, so God cannot indeed be seen by human eyes, but is beheld and perceived through His providence and works.
florilegium.gloss: Among the oldest forms of the argument in Christian Greek, written around AD 180 to a pagan friend, and one of the fairest. You do not see anyone's inner life either; you infer it from how a body moves and speaks. Theophilus asks only that the same courtesy be extended to God.

florilegium.author: St Justin Martyr
florilegium.text: For whatever either lawgivers or philosophers uttered well, they elaborated by finding and contemplating some part of the Word. But since they did not know the whole of the Word, which is Christ, they often contradicted themselves.
florilegium.gloss: Justin's generosity is doctrine, not manners. If Christ is the Logos, then anyone reasoning well is not reasoning outside Him but partly within Him, whatever they believe about Him. This is the reason a Christian can take an unbeliever's argument seriously rather than merely survive it.

florilegium.author: St Justin Martyr
florilegium.text: For each man spoke well in proportion to the share he had of the spermatic word, seeing what was related to it. But they who contradict themselves on the more important points appear not to have possessed the heavenly wisdom, and the knowledge which cannot be spoken against. Whatever things were rightly said among all men, are the property of us Christians.
florilegium.gloss: Written in a century when Christians were being put to death by the people he is addressing. He is still claiming, and not disowning, whatever the other side got right. That is the posture this whole topic is meant to be read in.

florilegium.author: St John Chrysostom
florilegium.text: For the conscience and reason does suffice in the Law's stead. By this he showed, first, that God made man independent, so as to be able to choose virtue and to avoid vice.
florilegium.gloss: Chrysostom's reading of conscience, and note what he does not say. It is not a divine implant overriding freedom. It is reason and conscience together doing the work of a law, in a man God made free enough to disregard it.

florilegium.author: St John Chrysostom
florilegium.text: He has placed His Creation in the midst, before the eyes of all men; in order that they may guess at the Creator from His works.
florilegium.gloss: Preached to a terrified Antioch awaiting imperial punishment, not to a seminar. Chrysostom's stress falls on in the midst: the evidence is set where the unlearned can reach it as easily as the wise, which is why he thinks no one is shut out of the question.

scripture.note: The fool hath said in his heart, There is no God.
In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.
The invisible things of God are clearly seen, understood by the things that are made.
He is before all things, and by him all things consist.
He is not far from every one of us; for in him we live, and move, and have our being.
They shew the work of the law written in their hearts, their conscience also bearing witness.
The heavens declare the glory of God; and the firmament sheweth his handywork.
By the greatness and beauty of the creatures proportionably the maker of them is seen.

editorialNotes: VERIFICATION RUN, WHAT WAS ACTUALLY CHECKED. Every one of the fourteen florilegium entries was fetched live on 2026-07-27 with curl (not WebFetch, per the standing warning about truncated pages producing confident false reports), stripped of markup, and read in context before being quoted. The draft was then passed through the repo's own gate: node scripts/audit-florilegium.mjs against a scratch copy. Result: kept=14, below-threshold=0, every entry at 100% in-order coverage with contiguous anchors between 23 and 40 words. Pages actually opened: newadvent.org/fathers/2801.htm, 32011.htm, 33041.htm, 2915.htm, 02041.htm, 0127.htm, 210205.htm, 190109.htm. All are NPNF or ANF, all pre-1929 English, all public domain.

THREE ENTRIES END AT AN INTERNAL CUT, punctuation supplied. Athanasius 42.3 stops at 'the unity of the universe and of its order' where the source runs on with a comma; John of Damascus I.6 stops at 'begotten of Himself' where the source runs on with a comma; Chrysostom, Statues 9 stops at 'guess at the Creator from His works' where the source has a semicolon. In each case a full stop was supplied at the truncation and nothing else was altered. No word of any quotation was changed, modernised, or reordered. Flagging because a reader comparing against New Advent will see the difference.

NO ST GREGORY PALAMAS. He is the obvious Father to reach for on uncreated Reason and the divine energies, and he is deliberately absent. The standard English of the 150 Chapters and the Triads is modern and under copyright, and there is no public-domain translation worth quoting. His argument is not paraphrased into quotation form anywhere in this file. If a future revision wants him, it needs a rights-cleared translation first, not a reconstruction.

SOURCE OF THE NEW MATERIAL. The transcendental argument, the intentionality argument, and the Euthyphro answer come from ChristosAnesti's #dogma-exegesis thread of 2026-06-11. His publication permission is on record (editorial-standards.md, clergy queue item 3, owner-confirmed 2026-07-27). None of his wording is reproduced; the substance is restated in house voice. The combative moves in the source were dropped deliberately and by name: the line that an interlocutor 'has not earned the right' to discuss comparative religion, the 'nobody sane' framing of the intentionality argument, and the passing shots at Thomists. A Catholic or an enquiring atheist should be able to read this file without being insulted, and that was the test applied to every sentence.

WHAT THIS FILE DELIBERATELY DOES NOT CLAIM, and this is the doctrinal judgment most likely to be pressed. The transcendental argument is presented as real and worth making but explicitly non-compelling. The three standard replies are stated at full strength (logic as convention, logic as abstract necessity, logic as brute feature), and the third one, that the theist has only relocated bruteness one step later, is conceded to be unanswerable by demonstration. The essay says in as many words that the Christian answer here is 'a judgment about which terminus is the more intelligible' and 'not a demonstration'. The evolutionary-debunking argument is likewise pulled back: the standard reply that selection favours accuracy is granted as 'largely right', and only the narrower point about domains far from survival is kept. If clergy or the owner want a stronger claim than this, that is a doctrinal decision and should be made explicitly rather than by editing an adjective.

EXISTING PROSE PRESERVED. The original five essay blocks were judged good and are carried over verbatim: the opening paragraph, the two paragraphs under 'What the world itself says', the paragraph under 'The witness within man', and the closing 'not a proof but a Person'. Nothing existing was rewritten. Everything new was added around them. The summary and subtitle are also unchanged, so lib/apologetics/topics.ts needs no edit on those fields.
